segments.segment_name: Opening: The Fog and the Wards in Chancery

episode_segment.title: Opening: The Fog and the Wards in Chancery

utterances.text: A literary companion to Charles Dickens's great novel of fog, law, and hidden fires.
I'm your host, and each episode we gather around the text like friends by a hearth—warm, curious, and close.
Tonight, we begin where Dickens begins—with atmosphere.
And with the first of our three guests—Dr. Sarah Chen, a computational linguist from MIT.
Sarah listens to Dickens’s sentences like a composer listens to a score—tracking rhythm, stress, and how meaning dissolves before our eyes.
Next, Dr. Rebecca Martinez, an observational astronomer based in New Mexico.
Rebecca brings the scientist’s eye—testing Dickens’s worlds like starfields, asking: what patterns hold? What vanishes under scrutiny?
And finally, Dr. Elena Volkov, musicologist and cultural historian.
Elena hears the novel’s pulse—its repetitions, its cadences, its quiet defiance against institutions that grind people to dust.
I’ll begin with the very first sentence of Bleak House.
Fog up the river, where it flows among green aits and meadows; fog down the river, where it rolls defiled among the tiers of shipping and the waterside pollutions of a great (and dirty) city.”
The fog doesn’t just obscure things.
Who is polluting? Who is defiling?
The sentence structure gives us no answer.
So the fog isn’t just weather.
Rebecca, you’ve mapped the long vacation of Chancery.
When the courts shut down, what do we see?
Let’s look at the passage in Chapter 19.
“The good ships Law and Equity, those teak-built, copper-bottomed, iron-fastened, brazen-faced, and not by any means fast-sailing clippers are laid up in ordinary.”
So even in dormancy, the system persists.
Elena, you’ve called Bleak House the house a political counterweight.
But Rebecca’s reading suggests it might just be a local pocket of warmth.

“with its light, and warmth, and comfort; with its hospitable jingle, at a distance, of preparations for dinner; with the face of its generous master brightening everything we saw; and just wind enough without to sound a low accompaniment to everything we heard, were our first impressions of Bleak House”
Each clause builds on the last—light, then warmth, then comfort.
It’s a structure that resists entropy.

segments.segment_name: Deep Dive: Richard's Unraveling—Ambition and Law

episode_segment.title: Deep Dive: Richard's UnravelingAmbition and Law

utterances.text: We've seen how Chancery casts its fog over the world of Bleak House.
Now let's follow that fog as it seeps into one life in particularRichard Carstone's.
Sarah, you've flagged something I want to start with because it's the kind of thing most readers just glide past.

In that c23:p37 passage'I wish to heaven I were a more constant sort of fellow, if I were a more constant sort of fellow, I should have held on...'you're saying that repetition isn't just Richard being self-pitying.
It's actually doing something linguistically specific.
What exactly is Dickens capturing there?
And does it tell us something about Richard that a purely thematic reading would miss?
Richard starts with a subjunctive wish'I wish I were...'
But then he immediately re-enters that clause as if it's a premise.
He doesn't complete the first thought.
The sentence folds in on itself.
And that's what's happening to Richardto his mind.

"I understand you, and I wish to heaven I were a more constant sort of fellow...If I were a more constant sort of fellow, I should have held on either to Badger or to Kenge and Carboy like grim death, and should have begun to be steady and systematic by this time, and shouldn't be in debt, and"
This isn't just him being inconsistent.
It's that his internal grammarhis ability to build a coherent lifeis breaking down.
I hear what you're saying about structure.
But I don't think this is just a neurological unraveling.
Chancery isn't just a background condition.
But he's actually being failed by a system that dangles inheritance like a carrot.
I wonder if we're describing the same phenomenon from different frames.
I see something more like gravitational distortion.

"So young, so beautiful, so full of hope and promise, they went on lightly through the sunlight as their own happy thoughts might then be traversing the years to come and making them all years of brightness. So they passed away into the shadow and were gone. It was only a burst of light that had been so radiant. The room darkened as they went out, and the sun was clouded over."
Like a star losing luminosity over time.
Elena, you've said something that I find genuinely provocative.
That Richard isn't inconstant by nature.
He's being *made* inconstant by the institution.
So when he says 'I wish to heaven I were a more constant sort of fellow,' he's actually misdiagnosing himself.
But doesn't that let Richard off the hook entirely?
Where does personal agency end and systemic destruction begin in your reading?
I don't think it lets him off the hook.
He's indicting the structure that shapes desire.
By a system that promises resolution.
Because the real ones are closed off.
Is the system the cause, or the amplifier?
But I'm not convinced it creates the instability.
Richard has a constitutional tendency toward volatility.
Look at how quickly he abandons medicine.
It gives that restlessness a direction.
Actually, I think both of you are partially right.
And we can see it in the language.
Early in the novel, Richard's sentences have embedding.
His speech is flat, recursive, lacking subordination.
The structure of his speech mirrors the erosion of his future.
But it doesn't tell us whether the cause is internal or external.
Only that the effect is real.
Rebecca, you want to read that passage in c13:p124'so they passed away into the shadow and were gone'as something like stellar death, a slow dimming.
But Elena is sitting here saying that shadow is institutional.
It's Chancery's atmosphere colonizing private life.
Are you two actually describing the same thing from different angles?
Or is there a real disagreement about what's causing Richard's trajectory?
I think we're using the same metaphor for different mechanisms.
It's just a machine that consumes energy.
Chancery exists to serve the powerful.
Its delays, its costs, its opacityall protect entrenched interests.
But the damage is systemic, not accidental.
Sarah, you mentioned something in our pre-conversation that I keep coming back to.
That in c51:p64, the death scene, Ada grammatically takes the main verbshe's the one kneeling, clasping, turning.
While Richard is syntactically backgrounded, almost dissolved into participial phrases.
Does that mean Dickens is encoding something about agency and personhood in the clause structure itself?
Because that's a wild claim and I want to make sure I'm understanding it right.
"my darling rose, put off her bonnet, kneeled down beside him with her golden hair falling like sunlight on his head, clasped her two arms round his neck, and turned her face to me"
Richard is the object of prepositions.
And I think that grammatical erasure is political.
The institution doesn't just destroy bodies.
It just makes the disappearance more tender.
And that's exactly what I mean by the last light.
Ada's hair falling on his head.
It's marking the moment before it arrives.
Like the final emission from a dying star.
We've seen how Richard is drawn into Chancery's orbithow language, love, and fate all converge on his dissolution.
But Richard isn't the only one guarding a secret.
Next, we'll turn to the silence at the heart of the Dedlock estate.
Lady Dedlock's buried past is waiting.

segments.segment_name: The Architecture of Secrecy: Lady Dedlock's Buried Past

episode_segment.title: The Architecture of Secrecy: Lady Dedlock's Buried Past

utterances.text: We've just seen Richard consumed by the false promises of Chancery.
Now let’s turn to another kind of unraveling—one quiet, contained, and all the more devastating for it.
In the desert, silence isn’t absence.
And that’s how I read Lady Dedlock and Tulkinghorn.
It’s a condition they’re trapped within—like gravity.
They can’t escape it any more than two stars can decide not to pull at each other.
Rebecca, you described Lady Dedlock and Tulkinghorn as particles locked in orbit around each other—which is a wild and kind of beautiful way to read a Victorian drawing room.
But I want to push on something.
You said the secrecy is a *condition* they inhabit, not a choice.
Elena would say it's a condition that was imposed specifically on Lady Dedlock—that the social system engineered her vulnerability.
And that calling it 'cosmic' or 'eternal' actually lets the system off the hook.
Does the astronomy framing risk aestheticizing something that's really just institutional cruelty?
It absolutely does let the system off the hook.
Lady Dedlock isn’t orbiting a secret.
And Tulkinghorn isn’t some neutral gravitational force.
Let me quote what Dickens writes about him at Chesney Wold.
He carries family secrets in every limb of his body and every crease of his dress.
Whether his whole soul is devoted to the great or whether he yields them nothing beyond the services he sells is his personal secret.
He keeps it, as he keeps the secrets of his clients; he is his own client in that matter, and will never betray himself.
I agree with Elena on the power dynamic—but not on the conclusion.
He’s a master of linguistic control.
Look at how that passage is structured.
But whether each evermore watches and suspects the other, evermore mistrustful of some great reservation;
whether each is evermore prepared at all points for the other, and never to be taken unawares;
what each would give to know how much the other knows—all this is hidden, for the time, in their own hearts.
He knows exactly how syntax suspends meaning.
But I don’t see a contradiction.
It’s not that the sentence *mirrors* the standoff.
And that’s why it feels eternal.
But because the structure persists even when the actors change.
But you can’t observe the center.
That’s showing how cruelty becomes structural.
The drawing room isn’t just a room.
And the silence is the space where those forces balance.
Elena, you said the real horror isn't Lady Dedlock's secret—it's that the price of existing in this world *is* permanent self-erasure.
But there's that line you quoted: 'Lady Dedlock is always the same exhausted deity, surrounded by worshippers, and terribly liable to be bored to death, even while presiding at her own shrine.'
That's Dickens being almost satirical, isn't it?
Is he sympathizing with her, or is he slightly mocking the performance she's trapped in?
Because Rebecca might say the irony is the point—it's what makes the suffering cosmic rather than pathetic.
Dickens sees the absurdity of the performance.
But he also sees its necessity.
And the performance must be flawless.
The satire doesn’t diminish her suffering.
She’s not just hiding a past.
She’s maintaining a fiction of self.
And that’s what makes it cosmic.
Not because it’s detached from history.
But because it transcends the individual.
And she’s trapped in its rhythm.
Like a star locked in orbit.
It doesn’t matter if it’s tired.
Because the forces won’t let it stop.
Rebecca, you said something in our pre-conversation that stuck with me.
That the most terrifying thing about hidden knowledge isn't discovery.
It's the possibility it might *never* be discovered.
And you spend your life frozen.
Growing up in the desert gave you a feel for that kind of isolating vastness.
Does Dickens's drawing room actually feel that way to you when you read it?
And—Sarah, Elena—does that land for you?
Or does the domestic setting make that kind of cosmic loneliness feel like a stretch?
Because what we’re seeing in Lady Dedlock is a kind of silence so total it becomes its own kind of noise.
And that’s a feeling we’ll hear again—softer, dirtier, and far more ignored—in the next voice we meet.
Coming up: the machinery of indifference.

segments.segment_name: Jo and the Machinery of Indifference: Social Critique in Bleak House

episode_segment.title: Jo and the Machinery of Indifference: Social Critique in Bleak House

utterances.text: Lady Dedlock’s secret is not just personal.
And that structure doesn’t just conceal—it consumes.
Now we turn to those it consumes most completely: the poor, the voiceless, the ones the law calls ‘irrelevant.’
A boy with no name recognized by the system—except as a nuisance.
Sarah, you made this claim in our pre-chat that stopped me cold—
you said Jo doesn’t just *sound* powerless, he’s literally grammatically prohibited from owning his own speech.
Can you read us that passage from chapter eleven and show us what you mean?
Because I think most people hear ‘He wos wery good to me’ and think Dickens is being sentimental.
You’re saying something much stranger than that.
The narrator begins with direct address: ‘Jo, is it thou?’
Then shifts immediately into reported speech—
not quotation, not free indirect discourse—but a kind of third space.
“There is something like a distant ray of light in thy muttered reason for this: ‘He wos wery good to me, he wos!’”
The narrator frames Jo’s speech as ‘thy muttered reason’—
It’s enclosed in the narrator’s grammar.
Jo never fully owns his own utterance.
He’s quoted, but not quoted *out loud*.
The law has already rejected Jo as a witness.
‘A rejected witness, who can’t exactly say what will be done to him in greater hands than men’s.’
The system doesn’t silence him by accident.
It needs him to be ungrammatical.
Because if Jo could speak clearly—
if he could testify with syntax—
But look at what the narrator does anyway.
He calls it a ‘distant ray of light.’
Like spotting a star through interstellar dust.
Elena, you said something in our conversation that I keep coming back to—
that the system doesn’t just *fail* Jo, it needs him illegible.
It requires his illegibility to function.
And you pointed to that parenthetical in the Tom-all-Alone’s description:
Can you read that bit and tell me why those five words are the most damning in the whole passage?
Let me read the full stretch.

‘Between his two conductors, Mr. Snagsby passes along the middle of a villainous street, undrained, unventilated, deep in black mud and corrupt water—though the roads are dry elsewhere—and reeking with such smells and sights that he, who has lived in London all his life, can scarce believe his senses.’
That clause—‘though the roads are dry elsewhere’—is the pivot.
Tom-all-Alone’s isn’t an accident of poverty.
Rebecca, I want to push you a little here—
because you described that moment—the cold night, the man turning to look at the shivering boy, sharing his supper—as cosmology rather than social critique.
But Elena is basically sitting here saying: Dickens is *colder* than that.
He’s not offering us that moment as comfort.
He’s showing us that the system sees that grace and *discards it anyway*.
Does the astronomy metaphor hold up against that reading?
Or does it soften something Dickens intends to be brutal?

‘That one cold winter night when he, the boy, was shivering in a doorway near his crossing, the man turned to look at him, and came back, and having questioned him and found that he had not a friend in the world, said, “Neither have I. Not one!” and gave him the price of a supper and a night’s lodging.’
But the narrative also shows the system moving on.
‘Never have a mission, my dear child.’
The system consumes even those who try to reform it.
Elena, let’s talk about Mrs. Piper for a second—
because all three of you flagged that passage and I think for quite different reasons.
You’re saying her testimony shows how rumor gets weaponized by systems—
But Sarah is saying her sentences literally don’t work—they fail grammatically.
Or are you actually disagreeing about where the damage happens—
in the structure of power or in the structure of language?
‘Why, Mrs. Piper has a good deal to say, chiefly in parentheses and without punctuation, but not much to tell.’
The language itself can’t sustain a coherent accusation.
The law gives her space to speak—
but only in a form that discredits her.
It lets the system claim to hear the poor—
Last one—and I want all three of you on this.
Sarah, you said the fog passage has no main finite verb for three paragraphs—
and that *is* the experience of confusion, not a symbol for it.
Rebecca, you’d probably say the atmosphere is doing something closer to spectroscopy—reading social anatomy.
Elena, you’d say the fog is a political choice, like the dry roads.
are you all describing the same machinery from different angles?
Or is there a real disagreement here about what Dickens thought literature was actually *for*?
The fog doesn’t just represent confusion.
The fog hides what the system doesn’t want seen.
So the fog isn’t just atmosphere.
what does it mean to live—
within a world built to erase you?
into the dust, the silence, and the faint but persistent light.

segments.segment_name: Themes of Entropy and Dust: What the Novel Asks of Us

episode_segment.title: Themes of Entropy and Dust: What the Novel Asks of Us

utterances.text: We've just come from Jo—the boy with no name, no home, no history—caught in the grinding machinery of indifference.
But now let’s widen the lens.
Because if Jo is one human particle swept along by forces he can’t see, what are those forces made of?
And a kind of moral entropy that eats everything in its path.
Rebecca, you’ve framed the novel’s atmosphere as argument.
So is Dickens saying these systems can’t be fixed?
That they can only be walked away from?
That’s exactly what I’ve been turning over.
Because the atmosphere isn’t just oppressive.
Let’s start with the room where Nemo dies.
He sees a man on a low bed.
But what matters is how Tulkinghorn experiences it.
Let me read you what happens:
through the general sickliness and faintness, and the odour of stale tobacco, there comes into the lawyer's mouth the bitter, vapid taste of opium
The opium doesn’t stay in the room.
And that’s how the law works too.
Let’s look at the narrator’s declaration:
The one great principle of the English law is to make business for itself.
That’s not corruption as a flaw.
And in thermodynamics, closed systems tend toward equilibrium.
So no—Dickens isn’t offering an exit.
He’s showing a system that wins by running down.
Sarah—Rebecca’s painting a system that consumes itself and everyone in it.
But you’ve said the violence isn’t just in what’s said.
And make us hear the syntax as force.
I’ll do more than read it.
Because the command ‘Move on’ isn’t just repeated.
It’s embedded in a structure that mimics legal procedure.
Let’s hear it as it’s constructed:
Do you hear, Jo? It is nothing to you or to any one else that the great lights of the parliamentary sky have failed for some few years in this business to set you the example of moving on.
The one grand recipe remains for you—the profound philosophical prescription—the be-all and the end-all of your strange existence upon earth.
You are by no means to move off, Jo, for the great lights can’t at all agree about that.
But also contradicted—‘move on’ but not ‘move off’.
It doesn’t just tell him what to do.
It enacts the legal system’s indifference.
And I was struck—immediately—by how Soviet that sounds.
They didn’t care what you composed.
The system fed on your presence.
When Richard and Ada come to her—

They went on in their own wild way for a little while—I never stopped them; I enjoyed it too much myself—and then we gradually fell to considering how young they were, and how there must be a lapse of several years before this early love could come to anything, and how it could come to happiness only if it were real and lasting and inspired them with a steady resolution to do their duty to each other, with constancy, fortitude, and perseverance, each always for the other's sake.
She doesn’t just bless their love.
These are the virtues the system rewards.
Or is she teaching them how to survive within the machine?
Sarah, you’ve been eager to get back in on Tulkinghorn.
Elena and Rebecca both want to quote that musical instrument line.
But you say it’s not just a metaphor.
As easily might the tone of a delicate musical instrument be inferred from its case, as the tone of Mr. Tulkinghorn from his case.
The first 'case' is literal—the instrument’s case.
The second 'case' is metaphorical—Tulkinghorn’s body, his manner, his clothing.
But the syntax refuses to distinguish them.
It collapses the literal and the figurative into one grammatical frame.
He’s grammatically indistinguishable from his container.
The man and the mask are syntactically fused.
But I’d argue the image works because it’s thermodynamically coherent.
A musical instrument in its case.
But a musical instrument isn’t meant to be played while in its case.
And the system rewards that performance.
So the metaphor isn’t about silence.
Rebecca—you asked earlier what Esther loses.
You’ve said her constancy extracts a cost.
What does the novel show us she gives up?
And in doing so, she stills herself.
To remain constant in a disintegrating world.
But to choose what you burn for?
We may not settle that today.
And follow Dickens’s digressions like a score.

segments.segment_name: Close Reading: Dickens's Digressive Genius—Form and Feeling

episode_segment.title: Close Reading: Dickens's Digressive GeniusForm and Feeling

utterances.text: We've been talking about dust as both image and moral condition.
Now let's turn to the forms that entrapment takesthe grammar, rhythm, and narrative devices that make Bleak House feel inescapable.
Rebecca, you said before we started that the fog opening reads to you like a protoplanetary diskprimordial material before any order forms.
Can you just read that first passage aloud and tell us what you're actually hearing when Dickens writes 'as if the waters had but newly retired from the face of the earth'?
Because that's a strange thing for a novelist to reach for.

As much mud in the streets as if the waters had but newly retired from the face of the earth, and it would not be wonderful to meet a Megalosaurus, forty feet long or so, waddling like an elephantine lizard up Holborn Hill.
That similethe waters retreatingisn't just poetic.
It's placing London not in history, but in deep time.
It's a condition of possibility for systems like Chancery to emerge.

Sarah, I could hear you tensing up just nowbecause Rebecca just called that passage 'not metaphorical decoration' and you've been very clear that what Dickens is doing there is grammatical, not imagistic.
What is actually happening to the sentence when Dickens writes that opening?
Rebecca’s reading is vivid, but it misses the syntactic core.
Let’s look at the first sentence.
London. Michaelmas term lately over, and the Lord Chancellor sitting in Lincoln’s Inn Hall. Implacable November weather.
It’s disorientation enacted at the sentence level.
Elena, you've described that fog passage as functioning like propagandamaking the system look inevitable, geological, not man-made.
But Sarah is saying the grammar is the argument, and Rebecca is saying it's about entropy and physics.
Are any of you actually disagreeing, or are you all describing the same thing from different angles?
Rebecca’s physics metaphorentropy, deep timeit risks naturalizing Chancery.
Making it seem like a law of nature.
And Sarah’s grammatical precisionit’s brilliant.
But it can’t carry the political weight.
It makes the system feel inevitable.
If Chancery were purely political, we’d expect clear villains.
Instead, we get a system that consumes everyone.
Even the Lord Chancellor is a blurred face in fog.
So is the physics metaphor distancing?
But it also captures how the system operates beyond individual intent.
Elena, you said something in our pre-chat that stopped me coldthat Richard doesn't fail Chancery, Chancery colonizes him so thoroughly that he internalizes its logic and starts blaming himself.
Elena, can you read the 'unfinished house' speech from chapter twenty-three and show us where that happens?
Where does it tip from description into self-indictment?

If you lived in an unfinished house, you couldn't settle down in it; if you were condemned to leave everything you undertook unfinished, you would find it hard to apply yourself to anything; and yet that's my unhappy case. I was born into this unfinished contention with all its chances and changes, and it began to unsettle me before I quite knew the difference between a suit at law and a suit of clothes; and it has gone on unsettling me ever since; and here I am now, conscious sometimes that I am but a worthless fellow to love my confiding cousin Ada.
Chancery didn’t just waste his time.
Sarah, you said Richard's speech is a *performance*.
That he's using conditional logic and self-deprecation to manage how he looks while he apologizes.
But Elena just read that passage as a man who's genuinely been broken.
Can those both be true at once, or does your linguistic reading actually push back on the idea that he's a victim?
They can be true at once.
The self-deprecation is both real and strategic.
If you lived in an unfinished house, you couldn't settle down in it; if you were condemned to leave everything you undertook unfinished, you would find it hard to apply yourself to anything;
'I was born into this unfinished contention.'
He’s still framing his failure as inevitable.
Which lets him off the hook for agency.
I wonder if physics can help here too.
Think of Chancery as a system with negative feedback.
The collapsing distance between analogy and self.
Sarah, can you read the moment they discover his remains?
And tell us what the typography is doing in that cry: 'Oh, horror, he IS here!'

Here is a small burnt patch of flooring; here is the tinder from a little bundle of burnt paper, but not so light as usual, seeming to be steeped in something; and here isis it the cinder of a small charred and broken log of wood sprinkled with white ashes, or is it coal?
The text doesn’t describe the scream.
We’ve seen how the novel’s form traps us as readers.
How its grammar, rhythm, and narrative devices make complicity feel inevitable.
But next, we’ll ask whether redemption is possible at allor those who survive.
Coming up: The Redemption That Remains Incomplete.

segments.segment_name: Closing: The Redemption That Remains Incomplete

episode_segment.title: Closing: The Redemption That Remains Incomplete

utterances.text: Last time, we lingered in Dickens's digressions—how his narrative sprawl becomes a kind of moral vision.
Now, let's turn to what that vision reveals: the slow erosion of a young man’s hope—and whether redemption was ever possible at all.
Sarah, you said something in our chat beforehand that really stuck with me — that by chapter 17, Dickens has made redemption syntactically impossible for Richard.
Can you walk us through what you mean?
Like, what does it actually look like on the page when grammar deletes a person's agency?
It’s right here—in Mrs. Badger’s assessment.
She says Richard ‘feels languid about the profession.’
He has not that positive interest in it which makes it his vocation.
No agent, no action, no volition.
The sentence doesn’t say he *chooses* indifference.
It says he *is* languid—like it’s a condition.
But Sarah—can we really say he’s stripped of agency?
He pins his future on Jarndyce’s kindness, on Chancery’s eventual justice.
I think Sarah’s onto something deeper.
In thermodynamics, we say a system approaches equilibrium not by choice—but by inevitable drift.
Richard isn’t failing because he missteps.
He’s being pulled toward entropy—like all things.
Elena, you called Jarndyce a ‘compassionate bureaucrat’—someone who treats individuals kindly while the machine keeps running.
But isn’t there a case that his counsel in chapter 13—‘trust in nothing but Providence and your own efforts’—is genuinely wise?
But it’s useless against the machinery of Chancery.
Kindness without structural change is palliative care.
And yet—his ‘if you DO change’ passage feels tender.
But let’s check what he’s actually permitting.
He says: if you find you are ‘more commonplace cousins’—don’t be ashamed.
If you DO change—if you DO come to find that you are more commonplace cousins to each other as man and woman than you were as boy and girl—don't be ashamed still to confide in me.
Sarah, you mentioned that the heathen waggoner line—‘never separate the two, like the heathen waggoner’—is linguistically incomplete.
Elena thinks it’s Jarndyce telling Richard to operate outside institutional logic.
Rebecca thinks it’s Dickens articulating something like natural law.
You think the incompleteness is the point.
Or is the ambiguity doing the work?
We don’t know who the heathen waggoner is.
The waggoner is outside the law.
He doesn’t separate Providence and effort—because he doesn’t live by Chancery’s logic.
He’s a natural system in balance.
Providence and effort—like gravity and motion—must coexist.
Last one—and I want all three of you on this.
Elena, you said the incompleteness of the redemption is the point.
But readers close this book and feel something—grief, maybe, or recognition.
If there’s no redemption and no cure, what are we supposed to do with that feeling?
Is Dickens just leaving us in the fog?
Maybe the fog is the point.
The grammar doesn’t allow for resolution.
Thank you, Sarah Chen, Rebecca Martinez, and Elena Volkov.
We’ve walked through the fog of Bleak House together—its syntax, its systems, its sorrow.
And perhaps, in that very sorrow, we find its enduring call.
For Bleak House Unpacked—I’m your host.
